data.title: 'I have no children': My aunt gave me $50,000 for a down payment. Now she wants me to leave my home to her two children.
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'The house cost $385,000. With my savings, her $50,000 and a small mortgage, I was able to close.'

"I've always planned for whatever I leave to go to my brother, a dear friend and a couple of charities I care about." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

Eleven years ago, my aunt gave me $50,000 toward my house, and I'm still grateful. I was 44, newly divorced and buying my first home on my own. I had about $65,000 saved but was short on the down payment for a three-bedroom in a neighborhood I liked. My aunt had money in a savings account earning next to nothing, and she said she'd rather see it go toward a home. She called it a gift and never asked me to sign anything.

The house cost $385,000. With my savings, her $50,000 and a small mortgage, I was able to close. Since then I've put in about $90,000 more: a new roof, kitchen appliances, plumbing work and new windows. The house is worth around $650,000 now, though that isn't cash in my pocket, and I still owe about $180,000. My aunt is 78 and has two adult children, a son,52, and a daughter, 49.

I barely know them. We see each other at Thanksgiving and Christmas; I send cards and birthday texts, and that's about it. My aunt has been a big part of my life. She helped me through the divorce, sat with me when my father was dying and stayed with me for a week after my surgery a few years ago. She has never held the $50,000 over me until now. At dinner last month, she asked me to change my will so the house goes to her two children when I die.

She said it isn't unreasonable and wanted me to consider her offer. She doesn't need the money herself. She just wants her kids to eventually benefit from what she gave me. I told her I'd always understood the money as a gift to me, not an investment in the house or an early inheritance for her children. She had a poker face, but I could tell she did not like my response. I don't want to punish her for being generous. But I'm not comfortable with that request.

I don't want to leave a house worth hundreds of thousands of dollars to two people I barely know. I have no children, and I've always planned for whatever I leave to go to my brother, a dear friend and a couple of charities I care about. I haven't thought of the house as a bargaining chip, just as the biggest thing I own. My aunt says I'm being too literal and that family isn't supposed to keep score. Now I feel gaslighted!

Am I being selfish for refusing to leave the house, or a good part of it, to my aunt's children?

Grateful Homeowner

Related: After 46 years working, I'm not retiring - instead, I take a vacation every month. Is that a good life in your 70s?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

The $50,000 was a gift, not a loan.

Dear Homeowner,

You are not being selfish. You have agency over your own life and finances. You are not being gaslighted. You are feeling pressured.

The $50,000 was a gift, not a loan and that, to split hairs, is being used as the bargaining chip. You can acknowledge that without agreeing to change your will. If you want to offer something, a modest bequest to her children is a proportionate option. Your aunt may not have meant to have come across so aggressively. Sometimes, people can feel embarrassed in the moment.

If you are uncomfortable about leaving her children any money, don't do it. It's far better to be uncomfortable with your aunt's request and her response to your answer than it is to be uncomfortable with giving money to people you barely know. It's your house - and you can leave it to whom you want to.

What now? Let's assume that $50,000 would be worth $216,000 in 30 years with compounding. You could leave each of her children $108,000, which is more than generous, and reimburses them for the money your aunt gave you out, with interest, assuming that the down payment reduced their inheritance. That's a suggestion, not a request.

You have poured $90,000 into this home to renovate, which has added value; you have worked hard over the last 11 years to pay off the principal and the interest; and you have taken pride in knowing that you have created a home that you can be proud of. Millions of housebuyers get help with a down payment, although it varies by generation.

Homebuyers frequently receive financial help

Four in 10 homeowners received financial help with a down payment on their current home, including nearly 80% of Generation Z homeowners, 56% of millennials and 35% of Generation X (which happens to be your cohort), according to a recent LendingTree survey. The percentage was much lower (12%) for baby boomers.

However, arguably it was easier to buy a house 30 years ago, as the price-to-income ratio has narrowed significantly. Depending on the study, the typical home costs up to seven times the median annual salary today versus just four times the median annual salary 30 years ago. That would explain why fewer baby boomers needed a leg up from parents/family members.

Your aunt definitely overstepped the mark.

Your aunt, for better or for worse, bided her time. You are now in your 50s and never had children of your own, and she has your home in her crosshairs. Yes, she has been a kind and supportive aunt, attending your graduation and helping you get your foot on the property ladder. In many ways, she has been like another mother to you.

If she were your mother, I could see a similar scenario playing out where she would suggest that you support the family cause and leave your house to your brother. But you have no children, and you have already decided to remember your brother in your will, and yet your aunt decided to proffer a version of that request. As an aunt, it doesn't quite land in the same way.

Children often ask the same of their parents

Lest we forget, these pages are rife with adult children, grandchildren, nieces and nephews making similar requests of their elders, asking what will happen to their estate after they're gone, and giving helpful suggestions about what should happen to the estate - which, surprise, surprise! - always seem to favor the one asking the question.

Asking the question is certainly a brazen, if not entirely unusual, state of affairs in families, especially if she considers herself a de facto guardian. However, she definitely overstepped the mark by indicating that leaving the home to her two adult children is the "decent" thing to do. That's a lot more prescriptive than just asking a question.

You don't have to feel ashamed about accepting her gift. Without your aunt's gift, you may never have been able to buy a home or it would have taken you many years. Yes, you are one of the millions of homebuyers receive assistance in the form of a down payment, mortgage payments and/or acting as a guarantor - so her generosity means you are not alone

What do you tell your aunt? You can tell her that you appreciate her help with the down payment, and you will give some thought, but that your estate plans are private. You don't have to answer to anyone. If she persists, you may wish to make it clear that being single and without children does not mean that you have to abide by other people's wishes.

Ultimately, it was a gift, and you can do what you want.

Related: 'We lived within our means': I earned $30,000 as a pastor and still retired comfortably. Why don't you tell people that?

data.title: Arrvel Expands Thermal Label Printer Portfolio for Businesses and Everyday Use
data.description:
Arrvel Expands Thermal Label Printer Portfolio for Businesses and Everyday Use

Arrvel Expands Thermal Label Printer Portfolio for Businesses and Everyday Use

PR Newswire

SHENZHEN, China, Oct. 10, 2026

SHENZHEN, China, Oct. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Arrvel is expanding its label printing portfolio with thermal printing solutions designed to support e-commerce sellers, small businesses, and everyday labeling needs. Combining compact designs with practical functionality, Arrvel's label printers provide convenient solutions for shipping, inventory management, product identification, and household organization.

As online retail and home-based businesses continue to develop, efficient labeling has become an important part of daily operations. Arrvel's expanded portfolio addresses these needs with dedicated printing solutions that help users manage labeling tasks across business and personal environments without relying on traditional ink-based printers.

Arrvel A42BT: Wireless Thermal Printing for Modern Workflows

A key product in Arrvel's portfolio is the A42BT, a 4×6 Bluetooth thermal shipping label printer designed for online sellers, small businesses, and home offices. Supporting both Bluetooth and USB connectivity, the printer enables users to print from compatible smartphones, tablets, and computers. The FlashLabel Pro app also supports mobile printing, offering greater flexibility for users managing orders and other labeling tasks.

The A42BT delivers print speeds of up to 150 mm/s at 203 DPI resolution. It supports both roll and fanfold labels and accommodates label widths from approximately 1.57 to 4.3 inches, with support for the widely used 4×6-inch shipping label format. These capabilities make the printer suitable for shipping labels, inventory identification, barcodes, and other labeling applications.

Designed for multi-channel sellers, the A42BT is compatible with major e-commerce and shipping platforms, including Amazon, eBay, Shopify, Etsy, and USPS. This compatibility helps users incorporate label printing into their existing order fulfillment workflows.

To learn more about our thermal label printers or make a purchase, explore our thermal label printers on Amazon.

Streamlining Shipping and E-Commerce Operations

Shipping label printing is a fundamental part of order fulfillment for online sellers. As businesses process orders across multiple sales channels, having a dedicated printing solution can help simplify daily workflows, particularly for those operating from home or managing limited workspace.

Arrvel's shipping label printer solutions are designed to integrate into packing stations, home offices, retail counters, and small business environments. By providing a dedicated device for shipping labels, these printers help users organize packaging tasks and prepare orders for dispatch more efficiently.

Their applications extend beyond shipping. Businesses can also use label printers to identify products, track inventory, print barcodes, display pricing information, and organize supplies. These capabilities make label printing a practical part of routine business operations.

Direct Thermal Printing Without Ink Cartridges

Arrvel's thermal printers use direct thermal technology, which produces printed content through heat rather than conventional ink or toner. This method is particularly suitable for labels containing shipping addresses, text, barcodes, and other frequently used information.

Because direct thermal printing does not require ink cartridges or ribbons, it can simplify printer maintenance and reduce the need to replenish traditional printing supplies. For users who regularly produce labels, this offers a straightforward approach to everyday printing.

Arrvel's thermal printing solutions support a variety of applications, from e-commerce fulfillment and logistics to retail operations, office organization, and household labeling. By focusing on dedicated label printing, the company aims to provide practical options for users with different printing requirements.

Beyond Shipping: Supporting Everyday Labeling Needs

Although shipping is a major application for label printers, their functionality extends to many other business and personal tasks. Arrvel's solutions can help users organize information, identify products, and maintain more structured work and living spaces.

Small businesses can use labels for inventory tracking, product identification, packaging, and storage management. At home, users can label boxes, folders, shelves, and containers to make everyday organization easier. Independent sellers and creators can also incorporate printed labels into product packaging and order preparation.

This versatility allows a single label printer to serve multiple purposes, making it a useful tool for businesses and individuals who need a convenient way to create clear, consistent labels for different applications.

Compact Solutions for Modern Workspaces

The growth of remote work, independent businesses, and home-based e-commerce has increased demand for equipment that fits into smaller, more flexible work environments. For many users, printing devices need to occupy minimal space while remaining accessible for routine tasks.

Arrvel develops compact, practical printing solutions that can be integrated into desks, packing stations, retail counters, and home offices. The A42BT reflects this approach, measuring approximately 7.2 × 3.15 × 2.56 inches and weighing about 0.86 lb. Its compact footprint makes it suitable for space-conscious workspaces, including home-based businesses and small-scale shipping operations.

Through its label printing portfolio, Arrvel continues to address everyday labeling requirements with solutions designed around practical functionality, flexible connectivity, and convenient use.

About Arrvel

Arrvel is a brand of Emdoor Information and a global provider of industrial technology solutions, specializing in rugged tablets and label printers for small businesses. Backed by a publicly listed parent company with over ten years of experience, Arrvel integrates advanced R&D, in-house manufacturing, and global logistics to deliver efficient, reliable products to customers worldwide.

Contacts

Official Website: Arrvel
Official Store: Amazon
Follow us on YouTube

data.title: 'I feel like a loser': My stock portfolio is swinging wildly. Is it finally time to worry?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'I presume these are sophisticated investors taking a profit'

"I haven't made any money in months." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I'm frustrated with the stock market. One day, my exchange-traded funds go up the next day, and the next day they crash. I presume these are sophisticated investors taking a profit. I haven't made any money in months. No yield at all. What to do? I feel like a loser. It would have been nice to be able to get a yield. Is anyone else having this experience? What strategies do you suggest for someone who is slowly and gratefully heading toward retirement?

Retail Investor

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: 'I'm never selling': I'm 47 and buy bitcoin with every dollar I earn. Am I crazy?

ADHD is on the rise, which mental-health experts attribute, at least in part, to our personal technology.

Dear Investor,

ETFs are traded throughout the day, but transparency does not equate to volatility.

Yes, they will fluctuate on any given day, week or month, as the news cycle pushes and pulls your stocks three ways from Friday. Yield, for the record, is also different from return; it represents the income generated - like interest and dividends - while return refers to the overall net gain/loss. Technology is all turning us all into checkaholics. We're up there with chocoholics. We want instant gratification, whether it's a boost of dopamine from checking ETFs, or a sugar rush from eating candy. If checking your portfolio is making you anxious rather than helping you make better decisions, STOP checking your accounts.

Focus instead on the long-term trajectory, which historically has tended to rise over decades. Forget about investors making money off microtrades. You don't need to beat those investors. Forget about them; they have nothing to do with you. Checking daily moves in your accounts gives you an inaccurate or, at the very least, incomplete outlook about the stock market's overall health. Here's a reality check. The S&P 500 SPX has risen roughly 14% from January to October, the Nasdaq COMP composite has increased by 18%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA has risen by more than 6% and the Russell 2000 RUT has increased by 13%.

Your anxieties are understandable. Tech and AI stocks are driving the majority of gains in the U.S. stock market. The geopolitical backdrop - the war in Iran, Russia's invasion of Ukraine and U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war - has spooked investors and led to fears of a recession, none of which have come to fruition. As you get older, the share of your portfolio invested in stocks typically changes to reflect the time you have to recover from a major correction in the markets (the "sequence of return" risk). That risk is particularly important in the years just before and after retirement: A large market decline early in retirement can damage your portfolio more than a similar decline happening many years later.

Don't miss: 'I don't want to die on the sales floor': I'm 67 and earn $19.50 an hour at a big-box store. When can I finally retire?

Seeking safety

A few broad strokes: Explore CDs and high-yield savings accounts (HYSAs) for safety, but you may have to sacrifice higher returns. Treasury securities and high-quality bonds can also play a role. You say you are concerned about yield/return. That's understandable. In that case, you should decide how much of your portfolio you want to devote to predictable income, especially if you're upset by the movements in your account, and how much you still need to invest for long-term growth so you can enjoy a comfortable retirement.

There are also psychological and behavioral reasons why incessant checking of your portfolio occurs - and why it can be counterproductive. Loss aversion, a term popularized by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, describes the tendency for people to experience the stress of a financial loss more intensely than the pleasure of an equivalent return on your investment. As a result, you may be inadvertently conditioning yourself to constantly monitor your Robinhood, Vanguard or Fidelity accounts. It's a toxic feedback loop!

Possibly of more interest to you, given your obsessive checking of our own portfolio: Shlomo Benartzi and Richard Thaler developed the concept of "myopic loss aversion," suggesting that the more often you check your portfolios, the more likely you are to notice short-term declines and also react emotionally to them. That's why people sell their stocks in a panic during a market correction and/or go heavy in gold, dive headfirst into bonds and cash vehicles instead, only to regret it later. Don't make a decision on Thursday because of what happened on Wednesday.

Don't miss: 'I'd rather be on a beach in Bali': My husband resents my $8 million net worth. Should I pay for his retirement?

Risk perception

Since you ask about strategies for alleviating risk or the perception of risk: First, take stock of what you actually own and when you'll need the money. If you're overly concerned about short-term movements in your portfolio, you could employ a dollar-cost-averaging strategy, where you divide the amount to be invested in vehicles - be they Treasuries or CDs - into equal-size contributions and invest them over a longer period. Dollar-cost averaging, for example, can make sense when you're investing new money and want to reduce the psychological discomfort of investing a lump sum.

A "bond-tent strategy" involves gradually exposing your portfolio's allocation to bonds in the years leading up to retirement, keeping a higher bond allocation early after retiring and gradually lowering that exposure later. The idea is to create a buffer against needing to sell stocks after a major market decline early, especially early in retirement. It can reduce your sequence-of-returns risk. As long as you have enough money to live on, plus a 12-month emergency fund, it's also worth figuring out how long your retirement savings will have to last and how much you expect to withdraw each year.

A "bond ladder" of individual CDs or bonds, on the other hand, matures at different times and can provide a more predictable income stream while reducing the need to sell investments at a bad time and reducing exposure to interest-rate and stock-market moves. A ladder can be useful if you know roughly when you'll need the money. Whatever you choose, your portfolio should have an age-appropriate mix of stocks and bonds, and cash equivalents. The right mix depends on your spending needs, other sources of income, your time horizon and - yes - your tolerance for risk.

Constant checking creates unnecessary drama. Sometimes, it's better to pick up a good book.

Related: I'm 71 and still working. I earn $108,000 a year. Am I doing the right thing?

NEW YORK CITY, NY / ACCESS Newswire / October 10, 2026 / New to The Street, the financial-media platform for public companies, pre-IPO companies and entrepreneurs, today announced that Show 775 will premiere tonight at 6:30 p.m. ET on Bloomberg Television as sponsored programming. The episode will reach business audiences across four global regions: the United States, Latin America, the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) and Southeast Asia.

Hosted by Jane King and opening from the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, Show 775 features executive interviews with Brent Nelson, Executive Chairman of American Fusion Inc. (OTCQB:AMFN); Dr. Sebastian Heinz, Chief Executive Officer of HPB (High Performance Battery); David McPhail, Chief Executive Officer of T-REX Acquisition Corp. (OTCQB:TRXA); and Alex Mouravieff, CEO and Founder of SyncMeOn.

The broadcast also carries television commercials from BioVie Inc. (NASDAQ:BIVI), Lantern Pharma Inc. (NASDAQ:LTRN), Big Sky Industrial (NASDAQ:BSIN) and FreeCast (CAST).

After the broadcast, every segment will be distributed across the largest YouTube ecosystem in the public-company space, the New to The Street TV and NewsOut channels, with more than 6.6 million combined subscribers.

"Show 775 puts four companies working on some of the biggest questions in the market, from where the next generation of power comes from to how it is stored, in front of investors in four global regions in a single half hour," said Vince Caruso, Co-Founder and CEO of New to The Street. "Fusion energy, solid-state batteries, the infrastructure behind digital assets and smarter restaurant supply chains are the kinds of stories that travel across borders. That is what our global Bloomberg footprint is built to deliver: No politics. No current events. Only Opportunities to Consider™."

Inside Show 775

American Fusion Inc. (OTCQB:AMFN): The Texatron™ Fusion Engine™ and the Power Demands of the AI Era
Executive Chairman Brent Nelson discusses the company's Texatron™ Fusion Engine™, an aneutronic fusion platform designed for modular, infrastructure-grade deployment across industrial, commercial, defense and grid-constrained applications. The conversation covers the company's growing intellectual-property portfolio, ongoing Texatron™ testing and validation, and preparations for a potential uplisting from OTCQB to a national securities exchange, as outlined in the company's September 22, 2026 corporate update. Learn more at www.americanfusionenergy.com.

Dr. Heinz explains HPB's licensing model, in which manufacturers build and run production locally rather than HPB constructing its own gigafactories, and why long-duration stationary storage, including the fast-growing power needs of data centers, is a natural fit for the technology. Learn more at www.highperformancebattery.ch.

Chief Executive Officer David McPhail presents T-REX's vertically integrated digital-asset business, which spans proprietary Bitcoin mining, data-center hosting and co-location services, crypto-mining container fabrication and mining-management software. Learn more at www.t-rexminingsolutions.com.

CEO and Founder Alex Mouravieff introduces SyncMeOn, an open marketplace and software platform that connects restaurants with food suppliers in real time. Mouravieff explains how operators can compare what they pay against available market pricing, discover new suppliers and connect directly in a more transparent procurement environment. Learn more at www.syncmeon.com.

NEW YORK, Oct. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ --

In 2020, founding partner Laurence Rosen was named by law360 as a Titan of Plaintiffs' Bar. Many of the firm's attorneys have been recognized by Lawdragon and Super Lawyers.

Details of the case: According to the lawsuit, throughout the Class Period, defendants made materially false and misleading statements and/or failed to disclose that: (1) Dick's cleanup efforts concerning Foot Locker's inventory were not complete, and, in fact, Foot Locker remained saddled with unproductive and stagnant legacy footwear; (2) Foot Locker heavily relied on legacy footwear products that were particularly vulnerable to intensifying promotional pressures across the athletic footwear industry; (3) in turn, Dick's was significantly exposed to an industry-wide environment of excess inventory and resulting promotional activity; (4) accordingly, Dick's was unable to achieve the sales growth, margins, and profits it touted to investors; and (5) as a result of the above, defendants' positive statements about Dick's business, operations, and prospects were materially false and misleading and/or lacked a reasonable basis at all relevant times. When the true details entered the market, the lawsuit claims that investors suffered damages.

data.title: AI Made Music Fast. CITY JAM Founder Pat Villaceran Says the Real Asset Is the Artist's Own Sound
data.description:
AI Made Music Fast. CITY JAM Founder Pat Villaceran Says the Real Asset Is the Artist's Own Sound

AI Made Music Fast. CITY JAM Founder Pat Villaceran Says the Real Asset Is the Artist's Own Sound

PR Newswire

NEW YORK, Oct. 10, 2026

As AI music races on speed and volume, CITY JAM's INDUSTRY.AIFF works on what no pipeline can force: drawing original sound out of human creators.

NEW YORK, Oct. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Generative AI has made music fast, and the race in AI music is now about speed and volume. Pat Villaceran, founder of CITY JAM, says that race leaves one input untouched: original sound from human creators. Drawing that sound out of artists is both an art and a science. It is the craft behind INDUSTRY.AIFF, which takes a label's signed-but-unfinished artists to catalog-ready work and carries them through launch.

"When you stack up the progress around AI, it's all about speed, and about getting human creators back on track. That is an art and a science of its own," said Villaceran. "There are blueprints in it. Anyone can copy a blueprint: the roadmap, the pipeline, the scheduling and the workflows. But you cannot force the sound to come out if it has to be an original sound. The creativity is in how you bring out and evoke insights from musicians and creatives, and that is what CREATOR LABS and INDUSTRY.AIFF do. How you do that is the expertise we have at CITY JAM."

In tech terms, the blueprint is the easy part. A release plan can be written down and handed to anyone. Software can run it. The sound, Villaceran says, cannot.

The figures show how fast supply has moved. Luminate's 2025 Year-End Music Report counted 106,000 tracks a day reaching streaming services in 2025, up 7% on 99,000 a day in 2024. In 2025, 120.5 million of 253 million audio tracks had ten streams or fewer. That is almost half.

A growing share of that supply is not made by people. On Deezer, fully AI-generated tracks reached almost 75,000 a day in April 2026, roughly 44% of daily uploads, and passed 50% of new uploads at the June 2026 peak. Yet AI tracks are 1 to 3% of streams on Deezer, and up to 85% of those streams were fraudulent in 2025. On Deezer, the flood is in uploads, not listening.

The CISAC and PMP Strategy study projects that generative AI "could put 24% of Music creators' revenues at risk in 2028." That is a projection.

The US Copyright Office is now asking what that volume costs. Its inquiry into music streaming fraud names, in its Federal Register notice, "the dilution of the royalty revenue pool" as the primary harm, and asks which industry practices may be "inadvertently contributing to streaming fraud." Initial comments are due November 23, 2026, and replies December 21, 2026.

Detection and enforcement sit with regulators and the streaming services. CITY JAM's work sits earlier, in the stretch between signing an artist and a finished record. The royalty pool is diluted by volume without an audience. Fully finished, genuine releases are what the pool is for, and those still depend on an artist finding a sound of their own.

So if speed is no longer the hard part, what is music for? Villaceran's answer is the artist's own sound. It has to be drawn out of the musician. Then the speed AI brings can serve an original sound instead of replacing it.

INDUSTRY.AIFF does this for record labels and artist services companies. It works with their signed artists from unfinished work to catalog-ready releases, and stays with them through launch.

INDUSTRY.AIFF sits within the AI-era accelerator and incubator model for music that Villaceran launched on October 9, 2026, starting with record labels. Artists get the kind of support a startup accelerator gives founders. Education and professional development sit alongside community and live jam sessions. Collaborations and commercial opportunities come with it, and so does technology.

About CITY JAM

CITY JAM is holistic, end-to-end infrastructure for the music industry, built for everyone from independent musicians to record labels and artist services companies. It runs INDUSTRY.AIFF and CREATOR LABS with a global network of experts and producers, including CITY JAM New York. Pat Villaceran founded and leads CITY JAM. She also founded the innovation agency The MooVe, and has built innovation programs for companies and founders in Asia Pacific and the United States as well as in the United Kingdom and Europe. CITY JAM brings that record to music. INDUSTRY.AIFF is CITY JAM's program for record labels and artist services companies, and the name of its weekday letter for music label CEOs. CREATOR LABS is a holistic support system for independent musicians. It is a separate offering and is not part of INDUSTRY.AIFF. CITY JAM is a brand of HINABI PRIVE, INC. For updates, follow CITY JAM on LinkedIn.

Media contact: CITY JAM, press@themoove.co

data.title: Real Estate Expert Mark Williams Explains What to Check Before Buying Land Near Greeneville in HelloNation
data.description:
Real Estate Expert Mark Williams Explains What to Check Before Buying Land Near Greeneville in HelloNation

Real Estate Expert Mark Williams Explains What to Check Before Buying Land Near Greeneville in HelloNation

PR Newswire

GREENEVILLE, Tenn., Oct. 10, 2026

The article outlines key factors that help buyers avoid costly mistakes when purchasing raw land.

GREENEVILLE, Tenn., Oct. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What should buyers evaluate before purchasing property in Greeneville, Tennessee? A HelloNation article answers this question, featuring insights from Real Estate Expert Mark Williams of Greeneville, Tennessee.

The article explains that buying land differs significantly from purchasing an existing home. Greeneville, Tennessee, buying land involves unique risks, hidden costs, and long-term considerations that can affect usability and overall value. Careful research before closing is presented as essential to avoiding expensive surprises.

Property access is described as the first critical factor to confirm. The article notes that buyers must verify whether legal access is provided by a public road, private road, or easement. Easements may limit how the property can be used or developed, so reviewing official records is important. Walking the land to assess slopes, terrain, and potential obstacles can also reveal additional costs that may arise when improving access.

A land survey is another key component in the evaluation process. The HelloNation article emphasizes the importance of clearly defined boundaries. If an updated land survey is not available, buyers are encouraged to obtain one. Knowing exact property lines helps prevent disputes with neighbors and supports proper planning for buildings, fencing, and other improvements.

Utilities and infrastructure play a major role in determining whether land is practical for its intended use. The article explains that buyers should confirm the availability of electricity, water, sewer, and internet services. In some rural areas near Greeneville, Tennessee, installing utilities can be expensive and time-consuming. Septic suitability and well water access must also be evaluated carefully before moving forward.

Environmental conditions and soil quality are presented as additional factors that can influence long-term plans. The article suggests walking the property after rainfall to observe drainage patterns and identify standing water. Soil quality can affect construction stability, septic installation, and landscaping potential. Flood risk and erosion concerns may also impact insurance costs and overall safety.

Zoning regulations are another important consideration when buying land. Local zoning laws determine whether property can be used for residential, agricultural, or commercial purposes. The article notes that setbacks, conservation easements, and other restrictions may limit development options. Reviewing zoning requirements early in the process helps buyers avoid disappointment after purchase.

Road maintenance responsibilities are also addressed. For properties located on private roads, buyers should understand who is responsible for upkeep and seasonal repairs. Shared maintenance agreements or homeowner obligations may add ongoing expenses. Clarifying these responsibilities helps prevent disputes and unexpected costs.

Financial planning is emphasized throughout the article. While undeveloped property may have a lower purchase price, preparing it for construction often involves additional expenses. Surveys, permits, utility installation, and infrastructure improvements should all be factored into the budget. The article explains that realistic cost estimates help buyers make informed decisions.

Finally, the HelloNation article highlights the value of working with a real estate agent and other local professionals. Experienced guidance can help buyers review property history, zoning details, and development potential. Professional insight reduces the likelihood of costly errors and ensures legal requirements are properly addressed.

In summary, the article underscores that buying land in Greeneville, Tennessee, requires attention to property access, utilities, zoning, soil quality, environmental conditions, and a current land survey. Careful research and thoughtful planning increase the likelihood of a successful purchase and reduce long-term risks.

What to Check Before Buying Land Near Greeneville, Tennessee features insights from Mark Williams, Real Estate Expert of Greeneville, Tennessee, in HelloNation.

data.title: Compact Gaming Freedom, Precise Performance, Richer Sound: Epomaker HE60 Hall Effect Keyboard
data.description:
NEW YORK CITY, NY / ACCESS Newswire / October 10, 2026 / The Epomaker HE60 combines a compact gaming-focused design with refined sound tuning and responsive performance. Built for players who value speed and experience, it combines precise magnetic switch technology, a carefully tuned acoustic structure, and versatile connectivity in a space-saving 60% layout.

Compact 60% Design Built for Gaming Freedom
The Epomaker HE60 adopts a compact 60% layout that saves valuable desk space while creating more room for mouse movement, making it especially suitable for FPS gamers who rely on wide and fast mouse motions. Despite its smaller footprint, the keyboard delivers a stable, comfortable experience through thoughtful structural design. The two-stage feet, rarely seen on magnetic keyboards, allow users to adjust the typing angle based on their preferred posture, improving comfort during long gaming sessions and everyday use.

Magnetic Precision Engineered for Competitive Play
Equipped with factory-lubed Creamy Jade Hall Effect magnetic switches, the Epomaker HE60 delivers a responsive typing feel with a slightly firm press, strong rebound, and clear feedback. Its adjustable Rapid Trigger with 0.005mm precision allows players to fine-tune key response based on different gaming habits, helping achieve faster reactions and more consistent control during intense gameplay. Advanced features such as DKS and SOCD further expand customization options, allowing users to optimize key behaviors for competitive scenarios. With high-speed input performance supported by both wired and 2.4GHz modes, the HE60 ensures every movement and command is captured quickly and accurately.

Tuned for a Deeper and More Satisfying Thocky Sound
Beyond speed and responsiveness, the Epomaker HE60 focuses on delivering a more refined acoustic experience. The Creamy Jade magnetic switches, tray-mount structure, aluminum positioning plate, and carefully tuned internal filling system work together to create a fuller and more concentrated sound profile. Through its five-layer sound-dampening design, the keyboard reduces unwanted resonance while enhancing sound consistency across every keystroke. The result is a rich, stable, and satisfying Thocky sound experience straight out of the box, without requiring additional modifications.

Flexible Connectivity with a Distinctive Gaming Identity
The Epomaker HE60 supports Bluetooth, 2.4GHz wireless, and USB wired connections, offering flexible switching between gaming setups, workstations, and mobile devices. Both wired and 2.4GHz modes support up to 8000Hz polling for low-latency performance, while the built-in 8000mAh battery provides extended wireless usage despite the higher power demands commonly associated with magnetic keyboards. Available in black and white color options, the HE60 offers different styles to match individual preferences, from a more performance-focused gaming aesthetic to a cleaner desktop setup. Its gaming-inspired ribbon design adds visual character while also making the keyboard easier to carry.

Price and Availability
The Epomaker HE60 is now available on the Epomaker official website, Amazon store, and AliExpress store. The keyboard is available for $59.99 on the official website.
